summary: Discusses the problems of using IP multicast in Differentiated Services networks, expanding on RFC 2475. It suggests possible solutions, describes an implementation model and presents simulation results. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Sending one message to many people while also giving some traffic priority gets tricky. This explains the troubles and offers ideas.

subtitle: The trouble with sending one message to many people while also giving some traffic priority

tldr.problem: IP Multicast lets one sender send to many receivers, and DiffServ lets networks prioritize certain traffic, but when a new receiver joins a multicast group, the network automatically gives that receiver the same priority as the original sender—even if no reservation was made for the new branch.
tldr.mechanism: When a new multicast receiver joins, the RFC proposes re-marking packets (changing their priority field) to a low-priority service at the branch point, forcing admission control and explicit reservation requests before the receiver gets the better service quality.
tldr.outcome: The solution preserves DiffServ scalability—no per-flow tracking in core routers—while ensuring that dynamic multicast group membership does not inadvertently steal resources from existing traffic.

facts.label: Implementation cost
facts.value: One byte per multicast table entry

facts.label: Test loss without solution
facts.value: Group 1 lost 50% of packets when group 2 joined unreserved

facts.label: Test loss with solution
facts.value: Zero packet loss; group 2 re-marked to best-effort

today: RFC 3754 is Informational and describes identified problems and proposed solutions for IP multicast in DiffServ networks. It has not been obsoleted. The mechanisms described—re-marking at branching points and using Limited Effort PHB for unreserved multicast flows—represent one approach to the multicast-DiffServ challenge. Modern multicast QoS deployments continue to grapple with these trade-offs between scalability and service guarantee.

sections.title: The Multicast and QoS Worlds Collide
sections.content:
The RFC addresses the intersection of two important but conflicting network technologies. Differentiated Services (DiffServ) provides quality-of-service by marking packets with a Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP) and having routers forward marked traffic through priority queues. IP Multicast lets applications send one message that the network replicates and delivers to many receivers.

DiffServ scales by avoiding per-flow state in core routers—instead, flows are aggregated by DSCP and treated equally within their class. But multicast creates a new problem: when a receiver joins a group dynamically, the multicast routing protocol extends the delivery tree to include the new receiver. Since the router cannot track per-flow details, it automatically copies the DSCP marking from the incoming packet to all outgoing copies—including on the newly added branch—without checking whether resources were reserved for that branch.

The result can be traffic contract violations: receivers who made proper reservations may lose their guaranteed service when unreserved multicast flows consume the aggregate's reserved bandwidth.
sections.eli5: Imagine a priority queue at a bank. People who booked ahead get served first. Multicast is like when one customer's request spawns multiple sub-requests. When a new sub-request appears, it gets the same priority mark as the original—even if it wasn't booked.

sections.title: The Neglected Reservation Subtree Problem
sections.content:
The RFC identifies and names the core issue: the Neglected Reservation Subtree (NRS) Problem. This occurs in two cases.

Case 1: A new receiver joins at a domain boundary node. The packets flowing to the new branch still carry the high-priority DSCP. If the egress boundary node meters traffic, it sees the aggregate using more resources than reserved and begins dropping packets to enforce the contract—but it drops randomly, harming both the reserved and unreserved flows.

Case 2: A new receiver joins at an interior node. Unreserved multicast traffic now uses the high-priority queue. Interior nodes have no metering, so they forward the excess traffic, which preempts lower-priority services and causes loss in those aggregates. Higher-priority traffic may actually increase beyond what was reserved.

The RFC demonstrates the problem using a practical test: two multicast groups share one path. When receiver B joins group 2 without a reservation, group 1's traffic suffers packet loss even though group 1 was properly reserved. Results show that B receives only 250 kbps instead of the 500 kbps intended.
sections.eli5: When a new group member arrives without a reservation, they're treated as premium. If enough new people arrive this way, the premium queue fills with unreserved people, and the truly reserved people start getting dropped.

sections.title: The Re-marking Solution
sections.content:
The RFC proposes a straightforward solution: when a new receiver joins, immediately re-mark packets leaving on the new branch to a low-priority or even below-best-effort service. This forces admission control into the picture.

The sequence is: (1) New receiver joins; multicast routing grafts a branch to the tree. (2) At the branching point, packets leaving down the new branch are re-marked (typically to Limited Effort (LE), a per-domain behavior worse than best-effort). (3) The resource management system is notified. (4) If a reservation is available or is issued, management instructs the branching router to stop re-marking and restore the original DSCP.

This approach scales because routers already maintain per-multicast-group state in the multicast forwarding table. Adding one extra byte per output link (to specify the DSCP for that branch) costs almost nothing. Re-marking happens only at branching points, not at all multicast nodes.

The Limited Effort PHB is key: it ensures unreserved multicast packets get discarded more aggressively than default best-effort, preventing them from unfairly consuming resources.
sections.eli5: New arrivals get a 'pending' ticket (low priority). If they later show a real reservation, their ticket is upgraded to priority seating. This keeps the priority queue safe.

sections.title: Supporting Mixed Service Classes
sections.content:
The re-marking solution enables heterogeneous multicast groups where different receivers receive the same content but with different service levels. Some receivers can get premium quality (if they reserved resources), while others get best-effort or limited-effort service.

This allows important use cases: a receiver might initially join with limited-effort to sample the content before committing to a reservation. Another receiver on a low-capacity link might accept limited-effort permanently. A third receiver, having reserved resources, gets full premium service.

The solution also addresses a problem that would occur with naive RSVP integration: in RSVP multicast, receivers must join the group to hear PATH messages before they can send RESV (reservation) messages. Without re-marking, this join message would cause the NRS problem. With re-marking, the join is marked as limited-effort and does not trigger violation of service contracts.

For any-source multicast (where any participant can send), the framework requires that each sender's delivery tree have separate reservations. This is inherent to the directionality of DiffServ.
sections.eli5: Premium, standard, and budget seating become possible in the same concert. Early arrivals can sample budget seating, then upgrade if they like it.

sections.title: Putting the Solution into Practice
sections.content:
The RFC provides a concrete implementation for re-marking: extend each multicast routing table entry with an additional byte per virtual output interface specifying the DSCP to use when forwarding on that interface. During packet replication, the multicast forwarding process sets the DSCP from the table, not from the incoming packet.

A management daemon (potentially using the COPS protocol) receives configuration messages that update the multicast routing table. Initially, new branches get the limited-effort codepoint. When a reservation is approved, management updates the table to restore the original codepoint.

The RFC also discusses deployment constraints: some specialized router hardware directly duplicates packets on the backplane without software intervention, making per-link re-marking impossible. For such equipment, alternative solutions include applying standard DiffServ traffic conditioning (classifier and marker) at egress interfaces, or performing the re-marking at the next downstream router.

The RFC also presents simulation results confirming that re-marking to Limited Effort (rather than plain best-effort) significantly reduces harm to legitimate best-effort traffic. When LE is used, best-effort flows lose only their allocated share (10% in the example), not more.
sections.eli5: Routers can be updated with software or extra cards to mark new arrivals as 'pending' automatically. A management system then upgrades the ticket if the reservation is confirmed.
